t: A conductor of resistance 3Ω is stretched uniformly till its length is doubled. The wire is now bent in the form of an equilateral triangle. The effective resistance between the ends of any side of the triangle in ohms is:
s:
The resistance of a conductor of length l, crosssectional area A and made of a material of resistivity ρ is given by
R=ρl/A=ρl²/Al=(ρ/V)l²
where V=Al is the volume of the conductor. Since ρ is a constant and volume V cannot change if the conductor is stretched, it follows that R is proportional to l². Thus if l is doubled, R becomes four times. Hence the new resistance is 3×4=12Ω. So, each side of the equilateral triangle has a resistance of 4Ω as shown in Fig. 12.127. Therefore, the effective resistance between the ends of any side of the triangle (such as side AB ) is equal to the resistance of a parallel combination of R₁=4Ω and R₂=4+4= 8Ω, which is given by
Rₑ=(R₁×R₂)/(R₁+R₂)=(4×8)/(4+12)=8/3Ω
Hence the correct choice is (b).

In the circuit shown, the current in the 1Ω resistor is
s:
Let the electrical potential at node Q be V_Q=0 V (due to grounding) and the potential at node P be V.
Applying Kirchhoff’s Current Law (KCL) at node P, the algebraic sum of currents leaving the node is zero.
The left branch has a 6 V battery and a 3Ω resistor. Moving from P to the left, the potential increases by 6 V across the battery (from the negative short terminal to the positive long terminal). The current leaving P through the left branch is (V−(−6))/3=(V+6)/3.
The middle branch has a 1Ω resistor. The current leaving P through the middle branch is (V−0)/1=V.
The right branch has a 2Ω resistor, a 9 V battery, and a 3Ω resistor. Moving from P to Q, the potential drops by 9 V across the battery (the positive long terminal is upwards). The total resistance in this branch is 2+3=5Ω. The current leaving P through the right branch is (V−9−0)/5=(V−9)/5.
Summing these currents:
(V+6)/3+V+(V−9)/5=0
Multiplying the entire equation by 15 to clear denominators:
5(V+6)+15V+3(V−9)=0
5V+30+15V+3V−27=0
23V+3=0⇒V=−3/23 V
The current in the 1Ω resistor is I=(V_P−V_Q)/1Ω=−3/23 A ≈−0.13 A.
The negative sign indicates that the current flows from Q to P.

For given values of E and r, power output P will be maximum if dP/dR=0 and d²P/dR²<0. Differentiating (i) with respect to R we get (with E and r fixed)

Now  dP/dR=0 if
1−2R/(R+r)=0
which gives R=r. Thus, P will be either maximum or minimum when R=r. To decide whether P is maximum at R=r, we find d²P/dR² at R=r. If its value is negative, P will be maximum. Differentiating (ii) we have

which is negative. Hence P is maximum when R=r.
